evidence_notes: Claim: driverless cars would not be good for society. Support: (1) they would make people lazier, given generally ('we already have sensors to help us with driving'); (2) a source detail from 'paragraph nine' about no one knowing who is at fault in an accident, extended into lying drivers and companies being sued; (3) there is 'no point' because drivers already know how to drive. Only the liability reason is carried anywhere; (1) and (3) restate each other and the claim. ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, opening and closing present, all three body parts relate; rung 5 fails - laziness, liability and pointlessness are interchangeable, and the third part loops back to the first without adding to it). DEV 3 (rung 3 yes on the paragraph-nine fault detail, the only concrete piece; rung 4 fails as a whole because the other two supports are general assertions listed for the reader to connect - 'most is general, listed not explained'). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: 'on one will really know', 'a lot companies sued because of car accidents and of people who do not want to tell the truth', 'we should not waste with something like a driverless car' all need repair on the way through; meaning stays recoverable, so rung 3 holds). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes - the liability reason says why it follows: unclear fault plus dishonest drivers means manufacturers absorb the blame; rung 5 fails, the opening 'they would probably turn out to be something great' is a concession never answered, and the closing redirect lands where the prompt's framing already implies).

Written as a staged dialogue between the writer and a friend. Claim: the Face on Mars is 'obviously just a natural landform'. Support: JPL's finding that it is a butte or mesa, 'landforms common around American West' (specific, source-drawn); the two-mile span making a living face impossible. Much of the exchange is personal attack ('something going on in your head that isn't quite healthy', 'I thought youre Mother raised you right') rather than support, and is set aside as not bearing on the claim. ORG 3 (rung 4 fails: the position is stated up front but the closing is the friend's parting threat, which stops rather than closes, and the middle drifts into insults that do not relate to the controlling idea). DEV 3 (rung 3 yes - JPL/butte/mesa and the two-mile figure are specific; rung 4 fails, the connection from the source finding to the claim is never stated, and the only gloss offered is 'that is just obserd', which is restatement not explanation). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: 'obserd' twice, 'wierd', 'everthing', 'youre Mother', 'than how do you sleep', 'I interfered' for interjected - errors accumulate and several spots need repair, but meaning is recoverable, so rung 3 holds). ARG 3 (rung 3 yes, the position is clear and committed and is the writer's own; rung 4 fails - the opposing view is present as a speaking character but is met by appeal to JPL and by ridicule, never with a stated why; the essay circles its position rather than reasoning it).

Claim: cars pollute and car-free living is becoming a reality we should move toward. Support drawn heavily from four provided sources: Vauban (70 percent of families carless, $40,000 parking, Heidrun Walter quote), Paris (partial driving ban, congestion down 60 percent, 67 percent diesel), Bogota's Day Without Cars (Cali and Valledupar joining), and US mileage data (peak 2005, 9 percent below peak, Ford/Mercedes rebranding, NYC bike share). Specific throughout, but most of it is reported rather than interpreted. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes; rung 5 fails - Vauban, Paris and Bogota are parallel illustrations of the same point that could swap places, the essay being a set of supports rather than a sequence). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes - the Vauban and US paragraphs state what the evidence shows, 'with Smart Planning, we can cut back on greenhouse gasses'; rung 5 fails because the Paris and Bogota paragraphs report source material with no explanation added, and borrowed material sits alongside the writer's sentences rather than inside them). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: the 'cold nights and warm days caused by the warmer layer of air to trap car emissions' sentence and 'diesel fuel is the mail fuel used in France' need repair, and spelling errors accumulate - expiremental, seperate, benificial, negitave, isea, county for country). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes, the Smart Planning reason says why it follows; rung 5 fails - the one counter-consideration, harm to car industries, is noted and waved past in a clause, and the conclusion lands exactly where the prompt's framing implies).

Opening claim: 'the advantages of limiting car usage are very rare.' What follows never argues that - it is a run of source facts (the 16-to-39 licensing drop, the $40,000 parking space, 12 percent of European greenhouse emissions and up to 50 percent in car-intensive US areas, stores on a main street, almost 4,000 drivers fined, 53.3 percent diesel), several of which cut against the stated claim. ORG 2 (rung 3 nominally passes on the first sentence, but the stated idea is contradicted by everything after it and never governs, so band 2(a) applies: no functioning frame, the text ends mid-list, and the parts stand in no recoverable relation to each other). DEV 2 (after discarding the fact dump, which is attached to no claim, what remains - people work to buy cars, kids get jobs for cars - is general; borrowed material stands in for the argument, the essay reporting what the source says instead of arguing from it). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails: 'other people who already have there license are renewing them' and 'stores are placed a walk way on a main street' force guessing rather than repair; sentences run on without capitals or stops, 'some people own cars some dont some take bus'). ARG 2 (rung 3 fails - the position is stated once and abandoned; nothing that follows is offered as a reason for it, and no commitment to it is sustained anywhere in the piece).

Written in a NASA voice. Claim: the Face on Mars is a natural mesa, not an alien artifact. Support: the 1976 Viking 1 photo of the two-mile 'face', mesas common around Cydonia, the comparison to the Snake River Plain in Idaho, and shadows producing the eyes/nose/mouth and the Egyptian-pharaoh look. Third body part concedes the resemblance and answers it. ORG 5 (rung 5 yes - the concession part depends on the claim-and-evidence part before it and could not swap with it, and the closing adds the skeptics-and-authors attention motive rather than restating the opening; rung 6 fails, the concession sits inside one part rather than the sequence carrying a nameable move). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes - the shadow explanation states what the evidence shows; rung 5 fails, several pieces are asserted without explanation, 'we have factual evidence', 'no for sure credible evidence', and the Idaho comparison is dropped rather than worked). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: 'It takes the shape of a face but also unusual shadows made it out to look like an egyptian pharoh when mesa's were more commonly found proving the face theory uncredible' needs repair, as does the doubled 'some scientist also believed it was indeed an alien artifact also'; spelling errors accumulate - suprised, belived, resebles, equivilent, suspition, physicl). ARG 5 (rung 5 yes - the strongest opposing consideration, that it genuinely looks like a face, is acknowledged and answered by the shadow-illusion mechanism plus the commonness of mesas; rung 6 fails, the answer leans on absence of proof and the prompt's terms are never changed).

Claim, stated in the first sentence: the Face on Mars is a natural landform, for three reasons - people cannot live on Mars, aliens do not exist, and only a head is there. Support: four quotations from the source ('There was no alien monument after all', the shadow illusion passage, the JPL web-site image, the Mars Global Surveyor 3D altimetry 'A mesa'), plus the writer's own claims that Mars has no oxygen and that gravity would crush bones. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes - idea stated first, held, opening and closing present, everything relates; rung 5 fails, the three reasons are interchangeable, two of them are crammed into one part, and the conclusion re-drops quotes already used). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes - connections are stated, 'That proves that the Face is just a natural landfrom... because', though the explanation restates the support rather than interpreting it; rung 5 fails, the oxygen and gravity claims rest on 'studies have shown' and the closing quotes are listed without comment). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: 'Mars has no oxygen so people can breathe' has to be repaired against its own later sentence, 'illusionb of eues' and 'why wouldnt the rest of the body by with the Face' likewise; landfrom, nautural, preasure, musles, becuase accumulate but meaning stays recoverable). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes - the no-oxygen chain says why it follows: no breathable air means no inhabitants means no maker; rung 5 fails, the alien case is dismissed rather than engaged, no qualification, no principle made explicit).

Claim: the Facial Action Coding System is unnecessary in a classroom. Support: three quotations from the article (the computer recognizing confusion or boredom, 'we humans perform the same impressive calculation every day', 'then it could modify the lesson'), turned into two worked reasons - the technology is redundant because teachers already read students, and modifying a whole lesson for one confused student is unfair to the rest, whereas individual help is not. Privacy and teacher salaries are asserted only. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes - thesis first, orienting opening, closing that closes; rung 5 fails, the salary, redundancy, privacy and unfairness points are interchangeable and privacy surfaces twice without building). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes - 'if humans already have this natural ability, then adding more technology... is uneccessary' states the connection and adds something; rung 5 fails, the privacy claim is bare feeling and the salary claim has no support at all). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: 'adding more technology into the classroom that teacher could already be doing' needs repair, nested quotation marks clutter several sentences, and uneccessary/invaison/instrucor/'In the article is says' accumulate). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes, the redundancy and unfairness reasons are genuinely reasoned; rung 5 fails - 'I am sure there are some upsides to this' is mention without engagement, and the closing scope limit, useful somewhere else but not the classroom, is a one-clause afterthought rather than a worked qualification).

Opens by handing back the topic - 'In this article author argued about to use the auto drive system or not' - and then reproduces the source almost continuously: the Tesla 2016 projection, Mercedes-Benz/Audi/Nissan by 2020, the Sebastian Thrun quote about sensors and mapping and radar, the 1950s antilock-brake sensors, and the source's own closing line about the road to the truly autonomous car, used twice. ORG 2 (rung 3 fails - no controlling idea is stated in the essay's own words, only a topic; the reader must assemble a stance from the body, there is no functioning frame, and the parts jump from 2016 release dates to a 1950s history with no recoverable relation). DEV 1 (the response is predominantly copied - almost every sentence is source phrasing, transcription errors included - which is band 1(d) and sets the trait at 1 regardless of how specific the borrowed figures are). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails: the writer's own sentences, 'Some people says it is dangerous but some people is not', require guessing rather than repair, and the transcribed text is decoded through percebt, mappuing, sensprs, advanxced, respong, druvung takse on theri own, we frow closer). ARG 1 (rung 2 fails - the single flicker of stance, 'Why would anyone want a driver less car that still needs a driver', is immediately contradicted by the copied optimistic closing, so no viable point of view can be attributed to the essay).

Claim: a driverless car is not a good idea, because it is laziness and a cost burden. Support: one realized concrete case on the concession side - a mother letting the car drive itself while she settles a crying baby - and on the negative side, a glance at the article about fault in an accident, plus speculation that insurance would be 'at an all time high' and that purchase and repair costs would 'break us'. No figures or named cases anywhere else. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes; rung 5 fails - the negative part raises fresh points rather than answering the positive part, so the two could be reordered, the negative part wanders across laziness, fault, insurance and cost in one unit, and the closing largely restates the opening). DEV 3 (rung 3 yes on the crying-baby case, the only realized example; rung 4 fails as a whole because most support is general speculation the reader is left to connect - 'it would cause more accident', 'another car problem that us Americans would have'). CONV 3 (rung 4 fails: 'who's fault would it be the would the accident be on?' and 'Only when the child is crying the can have the car driving it's self' both need repair; errors accumulate but meaning stays recoverable). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes - the cost chain says why it follows: makers compete on advancement, so prices and insurance rise, so ordinary families are squeezed; rung 5 fails, the benefits are conceded and then set aside rather than answered, most other reasons are asserted, and the conclusion lands where the prompt implies).

Claim: we should adopt the plan to cut down car usage. Support: 70 percent of Vauban's families do not own cars and up to 50 percent of greenhouse emissions in car-intensive US areas, both from source material; California smog as a visible case; the running costs of owning a car, given in categories rather than figures; and a fully realized personal account of a car accident that left the writer's father unable to work, closed with 'wouldn't you feel more safe in a bus'. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes - position stated in the opening and held; rung 5 fails, the pollution, money and safety parts are interchangeable reasons and the closing restates the opening's demand). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes - the accident narrative and the savings argument both state what they show; rung 5 fails because the money part carries no specifics at all and the 50 percent figure is dropped without interpretation). CONV 4 (rung 4 yes - errors are visible and frequent but almost all spelling, polution, liscense, detramental, extravogant, nerveracking, neccesary, definetly, and nothing has to be repaired to get the meaning; rung 5 fails since the errors are neither occasional nor confined to the minor). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes, the savings and safety reasons are genuinely reasoned rather than asserted; rung 5 fails - no opposing consideration is engaged anywhere, no governing principle is made explicit, and the once-a-week proposal is a practical step, not a qualification of the position).
